title: Four minutes
text: For years, running a mile in under four minutes was treated as a wall that human physiology had built on purpose. Doctors {{1}} that the heart might fail under the strain; coaches built training programmes around the {{2}} that it could not be done. On 6 May 1954, on a windless evening in Oxford, Roger Bannister — a twenty-five-year-old neurology student who could spare only forty-five minutes a day for training — ran the mile in 3 minutes 59.4 seconds, with two friends {{3}} the pace in turns. The {{4}} of the feat lasted barely seven weeks; the Australian John Landy ran faster still, and within a few years the four-minute mile was the {{5}} standard for elite middle-distance runners, achieved by schoolboy athletes before the century turned. The lesson is quoted wherever human limits are debated: the wall was never in the legs, it was in the {{6}}. Bannister himself resisted the {{7}} — he noted, mildly, that records fall when training, tracks and competition improve, and that someone would have done it eventually. But the myth has outlived the {{8}}, because it tells us something we want to hear: that the impossible is mostly a date that has not happened yet.

gaps.explanation: 'doctors warned that the heart might fail' — gave warning; ward takes 'off', warrant = justify.
'the conviction that it could not be done' — the firm belief; coercion = forcing someone to act.
'two friends setting the pace in turns' — 'set the pace' is the athletics phrase; seat is for chairs, and pacing or timing the pace would double the word.
'the novelty of the feat lasted barely seven weeks' — its newness; nobility = aristocratic rank.
'the unofficial standard for elite runners' — the recognised-but-not-formal benchmark; undue = excessive.
'the wall was never in the legs, it was in the mind' — a matter of belief; 'muscles' would merely repeat the contrast already dismissed.

gaps.hint: a reading of what it meant (noun)
gaps.explanation: 'resisted the interpretation' — the meaning others drew from his run; interrogation = formal questioning.
'the myth has outlived the rebuttal' — the argument that disproved it; rubble = broken stone, rebate = a refund.
